Title: When We Cease to Understand the World
Author: Benjamín Labatut
My Review:
I picked this book after I was impressed by the writing style of Labatut in the book The MANIAC. The writing style here is more feverish and hauntingly beautiful. What pains me is the fact that after the first chapter, the level of fictional elements interspersed with facts grows, and though it sounds beautiful to read, it might feel misleading. Although the way he creates those fictions is a beauty in itself...he paints them as if he is inside the minds of those scientists during their epiphanies, in the most romanticized way. The facts align with what I'd read earlier in In Search of Schrödinger's Cat by John Gribbin. Apart from that, those chapters are really elegant...especially the parts with Heisenberg in Helgoland and Schrödinger at the Herwig sanatorium, where multiple mystical passages describe their hallucinations and visions. These are really the most eerie yet elegant passages in the book.

Regardless of all that, it's a great read, and it justifies the title -- Labatut is speaking to that throughout the book.

Title: The Infinity Machine: Demis Hassabis, DeepMind, and the Quest for Superintelligence
Author: Sebastian Mallaby
My Review:
Yes, the book is about how Demis Hassabis became who he is, how he built DeepMind into what it is today, and how he envisioned AI at a very early age while being a chess prodigy. However, you cannot ignore the fact that the author portrays him as an almost saintly evangelist: a figure who never once had a flawed thought or misstep.

Still, it’s a great book if you want to learn how DeepMind came to be, and how Hassabis’s friendship with David Silver championed their research trajectory over the years, running from AlphaGo to AlphaZero, AlphaStar, and eventually AlphaProof. (While Silver no longer works at DeepMind, the book clearly highlights how profound his influence was.) You also get interesting insights into the inner workings of Google’s acquisition of DeepMind, alongside Hassabis’s perspective on the race to AGI through language models.

That said, as detailed as the book is regarding Hassabis’s formative years, it falls short when covering the Silicon Valley language model race from 2023 onward. It merely grazes over several critical milestones in this quest for superintelligence. Granted, I might feel this way because I’ve been closely following these developments since 2023 while working directly at the application layer of these AI models.

Overall, it’s a fantastic read if you want to trace Hassabis’s journey from chess prodigy to polymath, culminating in a Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside John Jumper and David Baker for AlphaFold, arguably AI’s most significant contribution to science so far.

Title: The Impossible Man: Roger Penrose and the Cost of Genius
Author: Patchen Barss
My Review:
The moment you reach the final page of The Impossible Man, you realize exactly why Patchen Brass chose that title. In this biography, Brass does a fantastic job of outlining the life of Sir Roger Penrose, leaning into a deeply poetic writing style - with a prologue that stands out as one of the most beautifully crafted pieces of the entire book.

What makes this biography so compelling is how it humanizes a publicly acclaimed physicist. Growing up, I often heard Penrose's name spoken with a kind of reverence, long fascinated by the impossible geometry of the Penrose Triangle. This book effectively overthrows that pristine idealization we so often force onto scientific icons. Brass explicitly prioritizes the human side and the inner poetry of Penrose's mind over strict technical rigor. While the book occasionally suffers from vague representations and oversimplifications of his complex theories, this trade-off feels entirely intentional. It chooses to expose the vulnerability behind the genius, showing how the sheer tenacity to understand the universe can force someone to walk a path of greatness that is inextricably bound to personal suffering.

Through intimate glimpses into his family dynamics and personal relationships, you see a man simultaneously in love with loneliness and desperate for companionship. A beautiful, recurring motif throughout the narrative is the concept of the MUSE, it becomes clear that after his detachment from Judith, Penrose was always searching for that external spark to anchor his internal world. Brass captures this beautifully, alongside Penrose’s lifelong obsession with puzzles and his profound, geometrically minded friendship with M.C. Escher.

Its a great read .

Title: South of the Border, West of the Sun
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
Like every other novel by Haruki Murakami, this one ends ambiguously, leaving the reader to construct an ending rather than handing them one. There is always a quiet sense that something magical or perhaps surreal is waiting just beneath the surface of his stories, and sure enough, the same happens here through Hajime's reunion with his lost childhood love, Shimamoto.

The way the story unfolds keeps you firmly grounded in reality while steadily building anticipation around the emotional dilemma Hajime is destined to face. By the time I reached the end, however, I realized I wanted Yukiko's character to be explored far more than she was. She appears only briefly, mostly through a single chapter and a few monologues. While the novel is ultimately about Hajime and Shimamoto, Yukiko remains an afterthought in Hajime's own narration until the conflict demands otherwise.

That monologue, though, was one of the most memorable parts of the book. It reminded me of the word SONDER - the realization that every stranger has a life as vivid and complex as our own. Although the word is usually used in the context of random people, the novel made me think about something slightly different: even the people we choose to spend our lives with remain, in many ways, unknowable. We become so absorbed in our own inner worlds that we often fail to notice the depth of theirs. Perhaps that is where human connections begin to erode.

Overall, this is a compelling and deeply introspective novel. While it doesn't quite reach the heights of some of Murakami's strongest works, it is nevertheless a rewarding and thought-provoking read.

Title: Sputnik Sweetheart
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
There is something strangely familiar, yet impossibly distant, about the way Murakami writes. Every time I pick up one of his books, I feel as though I am entering a place I have visited before, only to realize it has quietly changed while I was away. Before Sputnik Sweetheart, I had already read Kafka on the Shore, Norwegian Wood, Men Without Women, Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage, Birthday Girl, and What I Talk About When I Talk About Running. This novel carries the same unmistakable cadence i.e quiet conversations, solitary people, dreams that blur into reality, and an invisible melancholy that hangs over every page.

From the opening chapters, when the unnamed narrator begins talking about Sumire, Murakami plants a quiet certainty in the reader. It almost feels as though he has already whispered the ending to you. Yet by the time you arrive there, you realize you never truly understood what he was saying. This has always been one of my favorite aspects of Murakami's storytelling. He foreshadows not through suspense or plot twists but through mood. The destination is often visible from the beginning; it is the emotional journey that remains hidden.

The novel concludes in a way that many readers might find abrupt or even incomplete. Questions remain unanswered, characters remain suspended, and nothing resembles conventional closure. But I don't think Murakami was ever interested in tying loose ends together. His stories rarely ask, "What happened?" They ask instead, "How does it feel to live without knowing what happened?"

The title itself began to make more sense to me after I finished the book. Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, circled the Earth for a brief moment in history before becoming another silent object drifting through space. It feels like an apt metaphor for the characters. They briefly enter one another's orbit, alter each other's trajectories, and then continue drifting through the loneliness of their separate universes. Sumire, to me, is the Sputnik , someone who slips beyond ordinary existence, leaving behind only echoes. The narrator and Miu remain grounded, held captive by the gravity of her memory.

Then there are the dream sequences. No one writes dreams quite like Murakami. They are surreal without becoming incomprehensible, symbolic without feeling forced. They possess a strange clarity and as if dreams reveal truths that waking life deliberately hides. Their beauty lies not in elaborate imagery but in their simplicity.

One sentence stayed with me long after I closed the book:

"Understanding is the sum of our misunderstandings."

It feels like the philosophical center of the novel. We spend our lives believing that love, friendship, and intimacy are built on understanding one another. Murakami gently suggests the opposite - perhaps what binds us together is our shared inability to fully know another person. Every relationship in the novel is defined as much by silence and absence as by conversation.

Many people describe Sputnik Sweetheart as a novel about unrequited love, and it certainly is. But I found loneliness to be its true subject. Each of the three central characters experiences isolation differently. The narrator loves someone he cannot have. Sumire longs for a love she cannot express. Miu is haunted by a version of herself she can never reclaim. They are connected not by romance but by solitude. They continually reach toward one another, yet remain separated by invisible distances that words cannot bridge.

Sputnik Sweetheart is not my favorite Murakami novel, but it will stay with me like an afterthought.

Title: Love in the Time of Cholera
Author: Gabriel García Márquez
Additional Authors: Edith Grossman, Kjell Risvik, Carlos Marrodán Casas
My Review:
A prose that feels like a ballad.

There is something poetic about the way Márquez writes and this book is an example of that. From the very first sentence to the end of the book when Florentino Ariza says "Forever"...every page feels like it belongs in a song, melancholic and beautiful at the same time. Sure, as you go through the story you feel miserable for the characters...at times you even hate each one of them...but then again, at the end of the day Márquez is just showing what it is to be human.

Love is such a strong feeling to be tossed around casually, yet Márquez beautifully shows how love itself changes over a period of time. For different people it can have different definitions...for some it is stability, for some it is a constant ache that quietly exists in the very act of everyday perversions and for some it is simply a likeness they want to hold onto for as long as they can. What fascinated me the most was that no form of love is portrayed as superior to another...they simply exist because people do.

But beneath all of this I don't think the novel is merely about love...it is about time. Time is perhaps the greatest character in the entire story. Fifty years pass...people age...faces wrinkle...desires that once consumed entire lives slowly become quieter...yet they never truly disappear. Time does not kill love here...it transforms it. It sands away the sharp edges of passion until what remains is something almost unrecognizable from where it began. The love that Florentino Ariza carried as a young man is not the same love he carries as an old one...and the woman Fermina Daza becomes is certainly not the young girl who once rejected him. They are strangers meeting again with memories that have aged alongside them.

Fermina Daza after the death of her husband Dr. Juvenal Urbino finds a new kind of freedom again and sure, at moments when you go through the story you feel hatred for her, but at the same time you understand what must have gone through her mind. She might be wrong in the eyes of society as her son's wife points out...but at that age happiness always comes at a cost and Márquez paints a beautiful picture of how she loved Dr. Juvenal Urbino, though that definition of love was never as passionate as the one Florentino Ariza carried for her. It was quieter...built over years of living together rather than longing for each other...and perhaps that too is love.

What makes her decision at the end so compelling is that she knows exactly who Florentino is. She knows about his countless affairs, his obsessions and all the moral contradictions that define him...yet she chooses him anyway. Not because she has forgotten who he is...but because time has changed what she seeks from love itself. There comes an age where love is no longer about beginning a life together...it is simply about not having to end it alone.

And when Márquez writes that a woman can go to any length to sleep with the man she truly loves even if it means denying God...you understand the depth of the love Fermina developed for Ariza after her husband's death. It is not the love of youth...it is a love stripped of illusion. A love that has survived grief, regret, memory and the passing of decades.

By the time the novel ends and Florentino Ariza says "Forever"...the word no longer sounds romantic in the conventional sense. It feels almost defiant. After all, what is forever to two people standing at the end of their lives? Perhaps Márquez's answer is that forever was never about time...it was about finally finding a moment where time itself no longer mattered.

Title: The Library of Babel
Author: Jorge Luis Borges
Additional Authors: Erik Desmazieres, Andrew Hurley, Angela Giral
My Review:
I picked up this short story after coming across its name while reading The Short Stay in Hell. Since that book is heavily inspired by Borges' idea of the Library of Babel, I decided to read the source first. I would urge anyone reading this review to do the same. Read this story and then sit with it for an hour. It is one of those rare pieces of fiction that does not really tell a story as much as it forces you into a thought experiment.

There is no traditional plot here. Borges asks us to imagine a library containing every possible book that can be written using a fixed set of characters. This means the library contains all true histories, all false histories, every scientific breakthrough, every proof, every refutation of that proof, every account of your life, and every possible variation of it. Everything that can be represented in writing exists somewhere in the library.

What fascinated me was not the existence of this knowledge but the impossibility of finding it.

As I sat with the idea, my mind kept drifting toward some of the deepest problems in mathematics and computer science. The library immediately reminded me of Gödel's incompleteness theorem. The library contains every truth, but knowing that a truth exists is very different from being able to verify it. There is a gap between truth and verification. A statement may be true and present somewhere in the library, yet there may be no practical way for a human being to find it among the infinite sea of nonsense surrounding it.

The same thought pulled me toward Turing's halting problem. Even if a book contains the answer you seek, how do you know that your search will ever end? How do you know that the next corridor is not just another endless sequence of meaningless books? The library is full of answers, but it provides no procedure for reaching them.

I also kept thinking about computational irreducibility. Perhaps there is no shortcut. Perhaps the only way to reach a particular book is to traverse the library itself. This felt strangely similar to how diffusion models start with noise and gradually move toward an image. The destination exists, but there is no magical jump to it. The path itself cannot be skipped.

All of this eventually brought me to the P vs NP problem. In some sense, the library contains solutions to every possible question. The difficulty is not whether the solution exists. The difficulty is finding it. Existence and accessibility are not the same thing. Once again, the distinction between truth and verification appears.

What makes the story even more profound is the effect this library has on its inhabitants. Faced with the possibility that somewhere there exists a book containing the meaning of their lives, a catalogue of the library, or an explanation of the universe, many become religious. Others become fanatics. Others fall into despair. Some become suicidal. Borges seems to understand that when humans confront infinite knowledge and their own inability to access it, they often swing between faith and hopelessness.

What amazed me most is that this story was written decades before modern discussions around computation, complexity theory, artificial intelligence, and information. Yet it feels as if Borges somehow anticipated all of them. By the end, I felt mentally exhausted in the best possible way. Very few stories have made me think this hard.

I have a feeling I will be thinking about this one for months.

Title: Physics and Philosophy: The Revolution in Modern Science
Author: Werner Heisenberg
My Review:
This book was a difficult read for me because it was hard for me to reconcile the way Heisenberg seamlessly started associating physics and western philosophy ... specifically metaphysics ... The way he proceeds comparing the idea of self by the work of Descartes ... pointing out how "the Cartesian partition has penetrated deeply into the human mind" ... and compares that to the existence of the photon ... and then goes into comparing Kant's work to it and then the Greek philosophers is an amazing exploration ... but the fact is that it feels off and hard to read.

The chapter on relativity is one of the most amazingly written things in the book ... Heisenberg talks about the Copenhagen interpretation of QM and then goes onto relativity and starts going on about Newtonian mechanics and how it is a special case of relativity ... but at the same time he begins to define the tension between the combination of QM and relativity which is currently being explored with M-Theory and loop quantum gravity.

He goes on to also describing the fundamental tension in the idea of the double slit experiment and duality of the photon and how his own uncertainty principle stands ... hitting on that profound realization where he states, "what we observe is not nature itself, but nature exposed to our method of questioning." ... It really makes you question what's absolute and how a combination of different sciences converge in QM ... He also begins to explain space and time related to the Michelson and Morley experiment and the ideas of ether ... noting how "the concept of absolute time had to be abandoned" ...

There is no coherence of chapters and hence it becomes a messy yet beautiful chain of thought ... mostly because, as Heisenberg himself admits in the book, "we cannot speak about atoms in ordinary language." ... It's definitely not for people without some knowledge of physics because the ideas will confuse you ...
am still confused at certain parts and will be re-reading it again.

Title: What I Talk About When I Talk About Running
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
There is this paragraph towards the end of the book which perfectly depicts Murakami and his life and the quiet clarity he may or may not have intended to impart.

“I didn’t start running because somebody asked me to become a runner. Just like I didn’t become a novelist because someone asked me to. One day, out of the blue, I wanted to write a novel. And one day, out of the blue, I started to run—simply because I wanted to. I’ve always done whatever I felt like doing in life. People may try to stop me, and convince me I’m wrong, but I won’t change. I look up at the sky, wondering if I’ll catch a glimpse of kindness there, but I don’t. All I see are indifferent summer clouds drifting over the Pacific. And they have nothing to say to me. Clouds are always taciturn. I probably shouldn’t be looking up at them. What I should be looking at is inside of me. Like staring down into a deep well. Can I see kindness there? No, all I see is my own nature. My own individual, stubborn, uncooperative, often self-centered nature that still doubts itself—that, when troubles occur, tries to find something funny, or something nearly funny, about the situation. I’ve carried this character around like an old suitcase, down a long, dusty path. I’m not carrying it because I like it. The contents are too heavy, and it looks crummy, fraying in spots. I’ve carried it with me because there was nothing else I was supposed to carry. Still, I guess I have grown attached to it. As you might expect.”

This book is often spoken of as a meditation on running, but it is really a meditation on temperament. Murakami does not present running as heroic or even pleasurable. He presents it as something that entered his life unannounced and stayed because it matched the grain of who he already was. The same is true of his writing. Both are extensions of an inward rhythm rather than outcomes of ambition or instruction.

What stayed with me most is this idea of carrying one’s own nature without ornament or apology. He does not try to recast himself as kinder or nobler than he is. He notices his stubbornness, his detachment, even his self-centeredness, and accepts that this is the luggage he moves through life with. There is no self-improvement arc in the usual sense. There is only continuity. Effort is not used to become someone else but to remain fully oneself over time.

What I found beautiful is that he never argues that his way is superior. He simply traces how his life cohered around certain acts repeated for decades. Writing. Running. Solitude. Observation. Each reinforcing the other...

Title: The Life of a Stupid Man
Author: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa
My Review:
I read The Life of a Stupid Man by Ryūnosuke Akutagawa in the Penguin Classics edition, which includes three pieces: In a Grove, Death Register, and the titular story. Together they feel less like separate stories and more like different angles of the same quiet collapse.

In a Grove felt deceptively simple on the surface. The idea that truth is not objective is not new, but Akutagawa is not interested in philosophy for its own sake. What struck me was how every narrator bends the truth to protect himself. Each voice fights with truth not to uncover it, but to hide insecurity. Even the most “noble” characters lie, and they lie beautifully. By the end, it feels less like the truth is unknowable and more like it is unbearable. Truth exists, but no one can afford to carry it without distorting it.

Death Register was colder, and strangely honest because of that coldness. Akutagawa writes about the deaths of his father, mother, and younger sister as if he is reading entries from a register rather than mourning them. There is almost no visible emotion, yet a sense of reality seeps through. It does not feel cruel. It feels exhausted. Death here is not tragic or poetic. It is factual. The author looks at life with bare hands, not the careful hands of a craftsman shaping meaning, but hands that can only hold what is already there.

The titular story, The Life of a Stupid Man, stayed with me the most. It is fragmented, made of fifty-one short descriptions that read like the diary of a man already halfway gone. Early on, we learn that the narrator has written to a friend saying he may die, whether by suicide or naturally. That uncertainty lingers throughout the text. The fragments feel like a suicide note that never explains why he left, only that he was doomed from the start.

There is a strange, almost platonic love for death running through the story. Death is not dramatized. It is waited for. The narrator fantasizes about it, rehearses it, smiles toward it, even while the pile of responsibilities weighs on him. That smile does not feel peaceful. It feels like resignation. As if death is not an escape, but the only thing that does not demand performance, justification, or coherence.

Reading these pieces together, the book feels like a quiet self-indictment. Not a cry for help, not a romanticization of despair, but a record of a man who sees too clearly and cannot unsee. Akutagawa writes with a precision that slowly turns inward. By the end, death feels less like an event and more like something that has been waiting around the corner all along.

This is not a comforting book. But it is an honest and a hauntingly beautiful one.

Title: White Nights
Author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
My Review:
As Dostoevsky says, "How could you live without a story to tell?" The reading experience of White Nights counts as a story in itself. From the very start, Dostoevsky reminds us of the beauty of nights, and how even those whom the world calls lonely can find happiness. He compels you to feel what the Dreamer feels and think with a certain enthusiasm about how profound, yet pitiful, dreams can be as the Dreamer narrates his story to Nastenka.

Dostoevsky, with subtle words, directly conveys that a human's mere presence on Earth is meaningful. He doesn’t force you to search for a grand meaning in life, but instead asks you to feel the inherent symbolism embedded in existence.
Just as you grow comfortable with the characters and their budding friendship, Dostoevsky, like every great tragedian, reveals the true nature of love. He drags you through its murky depths. The confession between the Dreamer and Nastenka feels like the collision of two fragile hearts-grateful yet filled with agony. The Dreamer's words, "Why, oh why, must it be that the sweetest part of our lives is filled with nothing but fleeting moments?" capture this perfectly.

The longing for love, and the experience of love unreciprocated, creates a heart-wrenching narrative. Tears roll down your face, not because of dramatic events, but because even as you stand still, the Dreamer's pain seeps into the world around you. The heart becomes like stone, and the world outside reflects the story—colorless, old, and filled with the despair of countless crying souls.
Sure enough, Nastenka writes an apology letter, but for a Dreamer, "What ifs" are everything. To see the potential of a future crumble into nothingness is like enduring "a thousand biting ants," as your mind processes a storm of emotions. There are only two things a human can do-hope or try-but when, despite both, one is left with despair, healing feels like an abstract concept.

Dostoevsky makes you feel all of this raw emotion. He doesn’t force you to confront reality but subtly guides you toward acceptance of it. Love, he shows, is irrational, and attempting to rationalize it-just because we are human,is utterly foolish.
White Nights is a devastating story, yet one of the finest reads. It is a tale that reminds us that sometimes, the beauty of life lies not in its certainty, but in its fleeting moments of hope and despair.

Title: Ghachar Ghochar
Author: Vivek Shanbhag
My Review:
I picked up this book because I saw it in someone’s Instagram story saying it is one of the finest, tightly knit stories they have read, and hence I picked it up. It’s a short novella, and the greatest thing about the book is the way the writer, in a simple manner, showcases the decay of morality as the family comes into money and leaves you with an ambiguous question at the end ...whose blood was it? Was it a metaphor for the killing of morals, or was Anita or Suhasini really killed? Because before that, they casually discussed how to skillfully murder and get away with it.

The character of Vincent dropping one-liners is one of the striking things holding the narrator throughout the book, and the way the author goes on to describe the ant infestation at their old home in finer detail only showcases that money sometimes doesn’t change behavior... as we see the narrator killing an ant by the window in front of Anita without any thought, when the ant was simply moving on its own.

The way the author brought up the made-up word Ghachar Ghochar and ended the book with it is brilliant. It’s simple, elegant, engaging, and refreshingly haunting without stretching.

Title: Small Things Like These
Author: Claire Keegan
My Review:
I accidentally discovered this book while going through Cillian Murphy’s movies. I saw a recent Irish movie with the same title, and it said it was adapted from the novella Small Things Like These. Curiosity sparked, and I looked it up. Found it was a short read, so I decided to read it before watching the movie.

There’s quite a reflection here on what it takes to be human ...flawed, yes ...but still holding on to that sheer sense of right and wrong, of just being human. There’s a certain restraint in the way the writer tells the story, especially regarding the church and the place where the girls were kept. And when I finished the novella, I understood why.

The book is not about showing the atrocities or focusing on the pain those girls went through. It’s more about showing what an act of kindness can mean, what being human looks like , all through the eyes of a simple man, Furlong, who himself was a product of someone else’s quiet kindness.

You follow his mundane, everyday life through the story, and all around him are people subtly (or not-so-subtly) telling him to stay out of it, to look the other way. But in the end, he chooses differently and maybe part of that is because his own past, being a fatherless child, still weighs on him.
There’s a portrayal here of what it takes to be human enough. Just enough to do the right thing, even when no one else will. It's a small act, but that’s the point ,it shows what people are capable of, on both sides.The writing is beautiful ... simple, elegant, and deeply moving.

Loved this ...

Title: No Longer Human
Author: Osamu Dazai
My Review:
There is a certain part of me that is horrified after reading this, and the other parts are happy that I read this book. It's hard to grasp the way Dazai paints the character of Yozo, and he leaves too much ambiguity in certain situations, but his idea seems pretty clear once you begin to laugh at the cruelty of life. I am certain I am no lunatic, but I laughed at some points when Yozo and Horiki discuss antonyms on the roof and get stuck at "crime," and slowly Yozo connects it to Crime and Punishment by Dostoevsky, which is brilliant in such a way that the very next moment we witness the crime, and Yozo goes on asking if trustworthiness is a sin. This made me laugh for some reason, and I am sure I am not a lunatic.

A brief part of this book revolves around the idea of how being someone who fails to say "no" bears the heavy weight of being the "yes" guy and slowly spirals into the very outcast that society terms those people who say "no." The juxtaposition is that at the moment after such pressure, both fall into the same category, but one is drunk and unhappy, and perhaps the other is happy at 5 percent. By the way, I believe no one can be happy above 10 percent; it's a weird theory of mine. Dazai points out the very idea of how there is no such thing as absolute freedom and how inept we as humans are in understanding it. People will call this book full of misogyny, but I will say, why? That's just the perspective of the character who got played by himself while trying to play the jester for the world.

There are sections where I feel Dazai points out the very truth about society: that it is similar to the individual, and the unhappiness of society is the unhappiness of the individual. That really struck me.

There are parts where I feel that the character is more human than I am, and I asked myself if that carelessness drove him closer to death every time, why am I not able to comprehend just staring at the abyss? Consciousness, I believe, is the central plot of the book. The more you become conscious of yourself and the society you live in, the more you require the courage to just live every day. The greater the height of your consciousness, the greater the chance that you are no longer human....

Title: The Death of Ivan Ilych
Author: Leo Tolstoy
My Review:
This book was my introduction to Tolstoy. Over the past year, I’ve grown into a fan of classic literature ....having read Camus, Dostoevsky, Kafka, Wilde, and Hemingway. Each of them has left me sitting in silence for hours after finishing, lost in thought. Tolstoy is no different ... but in some ways, he goes deeper.

With The Death of Ivan Ilyich, Tolstoy asks a devastating question: what if the life you lived ...the one you carefully shaped to meet society’s ideals ... was the wrong one all along? And how do you examine a life when you were the one making all the decisions? How can you judge your own self honestly when you’ve built your identity around pleasing others?

This book confronts that unbearable realization ...that the pursuit of societal “perfection” might be a betrayal of your true self. That the family you built, the career you chased, and the comfort you accumulated might be meaningless in the face of death.
Ivan begins to hate the very people closest to him ... not because they are cruel, but because they refuse to acknowledge the truth of his suffering. Everyone plays along with the illusion: the doctors, pretending they can help; the family, pretending they care more than they fear his death. They all want it to be over .... but won’t say it.
Tolstoy doesn’t allow you to read passively. He forces you to feel the physical and spiritual agony of Ivan’s slow decline. The pages gnaw at you with the same dread and pain that Ivan himself feels. And yet, somehow, the ending isn’t bleak ... it’s transcendent.
When Ivan finally accepts death, not just mentally, but completely ... he finds peace. He ‘sees light’. And in that moment, he defeats death by embracing it.
It’s a short book, and yes... some phrases are archaic or hard to grasp (a quick Google or a GPT chat helps!) but it’s more than worth it.

Title: Heaven
Author: Mieko Kawakami
My Review:
Finished this in one go and I don’t even know what to feel. It’s like Kawakami said nothing yet said everything. How what we do doesn’t make a difference. How there’s no such thing as right or wrong .....people do what they like and what they can. The whole concept of morality feels like a vague term we cling to until it collapses under the weight of reality.

The bullying ....brutal, vivid, extreme to the point where you almost want to look away ...but she makes you watch. And it’s not for justice or redemption. It’s just cruelty, naked, sitting there. There’s no hero’s arc here. No revenge. Just the machinery of human behavior laid bare:

“People act because they can, not because it’s right. Sympathy is fleeting. The system always resets.”

Kojima’s philosophy was almost a religion ...to live and die outside their world, to reject the “normal” entirely. But then the park. The nakedness. People seeing them. The shame. And then she’s gone, completely gone.

And he ....he decides to fix his eyes. That small act is like a betrayal of her creed. She would have called it surrender. And yet ...“when he sees the leaves for the first time, perfectly, he feels joy.” It doesn’t solve anything. Doesn’t erase the cruelty. Doesn’t bring her back. But it’s his moment. A quiet kind of survival.

It’s almost like the book says: nothing matters, and this matters. Both at the same time. No grand answer, no moral victory. Just a boy, alone, looking at leaves and being happy. After everything.

In a world that doesn’t care, you take the small, clear things when they come. Even if they’re only for you.

Title: Acts of God
Author: Kanan Gill
My Review:
How do you tell people that everything is doomed, absurd, and meaningless... but still worth enduring because, in the end, your only real options are to die or accept and live? Kanan Gill attempts to wrap this existential dilemma in a weirdly charming, satirical, and speculative sci-fi shell.

The first 150 pages? Frankly, they felt like filler, overstretched, self-indulgent at times. But then the pace picks up, the tone sharpens, and the absurdity begins to reveal its structure. It's less of a story and more of a story being told to you ,a deliberate, fourth-wall-bending narrative that makes you question not just what you're reading, but why you’re reading it.

Gill doesn’t stick to linearity or narrative comfort. He throws in a talking wall, a cryptic pin that reveals life’s dumbest secrets, and characters like Manjunath, Heng, and the oddly divine Dr. K. Krishna ..... as in, yes, that Krishna. A clever nod to the controller/God trope, it teases out questions around simulation theory, fate, and the illusion of choice.

And then there’s this paragraph ...by far the most striking line in the book:

“Questions are only asked to know answers. And if the ultimate truth explodes the reality, then salvation is destruction. If truth is meant to be found, then everything was created to be destroyed. If the truth is destruction, then let destruction be true.”

That’s it; that’s the heart of the book. Satire camouflaging nihilism. Atheism playing footsie with Pascal’s Wager. A simulation where people start worshipping a half-baked police speech as divine prophecy ....because we’re always desperate to derive meaning from chaos, even if it's nonsense.

There's irony here: I'm unpacking the author's words with the same reverence he mocks. But that’s the trap. The book knows you’ll do this. That’s the game.

Not a book for everyone. Definitely not something you’ll read twice. But if you’re into absurdist thought experiments injected with humor, science, and unapologetic stupidity, this is a ride worth taking.

Title: Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
Author: Robert Louis Stevenson
Additional Authors: Vladimir Nabokov, Dan Chaon, Jerome Charyn, Simon Vestdijk
My Review:
I just finished reading this damn masterpiece and I’m genuinely shaken. Not because it’s horror...no. Because of how terrifyingly true it is. The whole idea that one man can carry both extremes..good and evil....in his chest... through a goddamn murder story. Stevenson doesn’t just write a tale; he opens your brain, picks apart your morals, and throws them back at you.

Jekyll was a doctor. A man of logic, a man of knowledge. But curiosity? That thing devoured him. He wanted to remove evil...but what he really did? He gave it a face. A body. A freedom. Hyde wasn’t an accident. He was a f**king craving. A bloodrush. And the second Jekyll tasted that high of doing wrong without judgment....he was hooked.

Jekyll didn’t want to eliminate evil. He wanted to separate it, tame it, control it, maybe even indulge it without consequence. That’s the kicker. He wasn’t after purity. He was after freedom from guilt.

And that right there....that’s the scariest part. Because humans? We're not born saints. We’re powerhouses of evil. The sense of goodness is just a social shroud. We behave 'cause we’re being watched. Because image matters. Because we’re scared. Conscience? That bitch shows up late. Or worse...shows up weak. It never truly stops the monster.

This hit me even harder because it echoes The Picture of Dorian Gray. That whole public virtue and private vice dynamic. Dorian and Jekyll? Two sides of the same cursed coin. Dorian hides his rot in a painting while Jekyll hides behind Hyde. Both are addicted to sin, to freedom, to the thrill of being unshackled. Both pretend to be noble in public while they rot in private. And both are torn apart by the very thing they tried to control.

You think Lanyon and Utterson are saints? Nah. They’ve got darkness too. They just wore stronger masks. Their rationality saved them...for now.
And the fact that a doctor...someone trained to understand the mind and body....gave in so fast, so willingly? That shook me. He didn’t kill the monster. He became it. You play with the monster, and the monster plays you back. Hard. There’s no walking out clean.
This story is truth in disguise. You want to understand people? You want to understand yourself? Read this. Not for the plot. Not for the twist. But for the mirror it shoves in your face.

If you're expecting a clean "good vs. evil" narrative....walk away. But if you're ready to look evil dead in the eye and realize it's been you all along.....then welcome to Jekyll’s club.

Title: Animal Farm
Author: George Orwell
My Review:
it’s a sharp, unsettling reflection of how power twists itself into tyranny. What starts as an idealistic revolution crumbles into the same oppression it sought to escape. The commandments change, the pigs walk on two legs, and soon, the rulers and the ruled are no different from what came before. The cycle repeats. There is no alternative.

Orwell’s brilliance lies not just in his storytelling but in his satire—naming the head pig Napoleon isn’t accidental. It’s a mocking nod to how revolutions eat themselves, how leaders rise claiming to free the people only to chain them differently. And the masses? Orwell shows them as forgetful, illusioned, willing to believe whatever version of the truth is fed to them. Boxer’s fate proves it all. The loyal, the hardworking, the ones who believe in the system—they are the first to be sacrificed. They don’t rise; they are used. Orwell exposes the brutal truth:

Revolutions don’t fail because the ideas are wrong, but because people stay the same.

Communism, as Marx envisioned, sought to liberate the oppressed but did so by turning against the rich. Power cannot exist without an enemy, and Orwell masterfully shows how every system—no matter how noble—creates its scapegoat to survive. It’s the same cunning Wilde captured through Lord Henry in Dorian Gray—strength, not fairness, is what people truly desire. Napoleon, like every ruler who thrives, understands this. The animals don’t just accept tyranny; they need it. They don’t seek justice; they seek control wrapped in the illusion of justice.

Orwell doesn’t offer hope. He offers reality. And that’s the best thing about his book.

Title: The Stranger
Author: Albert Camus
My Review:
Camus paints a philosophy that feels so bleak yet so right. It’s unsettling, and this is going to be long so its your wish to read or not...

I understand why people talk a lot about this book. Camus introduces a character so practical that he chooses to weigh every moment of his life logically, and honestly, that felt right to me. The very thought of questioning every belief that society forces into our heads feels liberating. People might call Mersault emotionally detached, but I don’t think that’s entirely true. From the very beginning,when the book opens with his ambiguous reaction to his mother’s death....it’s not that he doesn’t feel anything. It’s that he refuses to perform emotions just because society demands it. That alone sets the tone for the kind of life he chooses to live.

As the story proceeds, we see Mersault finding comfort in Marie. It’s not love in the traditional sense, but something logical,he enjoys being with her because they share simple pleasures like swimming and walking. It’s like his logical mind sought companionship for no grand reason but because it made life feel more tangible. Even in prison, he reflects on this simplicity, not with regret but with an almost detached acceptance of what he lost. His prison time wasn’t just about missing her or the outside world; it was where he confronted the truth that death is the one constant for every living thing. And somehow, he finds peace in that,not fighting it or resisting it but accepting it fully. That might seem absurd, but it’s also freeing. To live without needing a bigger purpose or false hope, on your terms, is probably the most honest way to live.....

The first conversation with the judge hits hard.... It shows how unsettling it is for society when someone like Mersault questions the very idea of God. To the judge, faith is a pillar of hope, something that makes life bearable, but to Mersault, it’s just another illusion. When society sees someone content without that illusion, they feel threatened. It’s as if Mersault’s existence challenges the foundation of their beliefs, and the trial isn’t just about the crime,it’s a reflection of how the masses need conformity to feel secure.
The jail conversation with the priest only adds to this. Mersault doesn’t hate him or argue; he just doesn’t see the point of clinging to something he doesn’t believe in. His calm rejection of hope as society defines it is what makes his character so powerful. It’s not that he’s hopeless,it’s that he sees hope in accepting life and death as they are, without needing to dress them up with meaning that isn’t there.

The ending disturbed me, though, and I think that’s the point. When Mersault hopes for something at the very end,not for mercy(though he thougt about existence of any possibility to escape), but for the crowd to greet him with cries of hatred;it’s unsettling. But when I thought about it, it made sense. It’s not really hope in the conventional sense; it’s almost like a final act of rebellion. By embracing absurdity, he’s showing the world what it means to live authentically. He’s not trying to teach society anything, but his existence itself becomes the question,the challenge to everything they believe in.
I want to reread it and may be i will find some other new meaning or ideas...

Title: Bobok
Author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
My Review:
This story is not the classic Dostoevsky you find in White Nights or Crime and Punishment. Bobok offers a sarcastic, almost grotesque view of the world, seen through the lens of both the dead and the living. Dostoevsky seems to suggest that while death is inevitable for every mortal, it brings no peace. In fact, peace is never truly achieved,it’s only realized in moments, much like how the arrival of winter is felt at the end of October, when spooky nights send chills down your spine. Mortals stare at the sky, hoping for meaning, while the moon stares back with a wide, blank eye, as if mocking them with an undertone of laughter.

In Bobok, Dostoevsky drives this point home by showing that even in the afterlife, people cling to the same trivialities that consumed them in life. The dead gossip, lie, and obsess over meaningless concerns, proving that the absurdities of existence don’t end with death. Peace is not found in death because human nature remains unchanged,even in the grave, people continue to distract themselves with petty nonsense.

To live and lie become synonymous in this story, and Dostoevsky captures that beautifully with an abstract boldness. His strange and often unsettling choices might not make sense on the first read, but as you sit with the story, you begin to understand why he wrote it the way he did. It’s almost like speaking utter nonsense but somehow making sense of it-an approach that seems far-fetched, but it works.

Title: Kafka on the Shore
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
where do I even start with this mind-bending book? Murakami's got this way of writing that just... it messes with your head, you know? Like, you're reading along, thinking you've got a handle on things, and then wham - he throws in some talking cats or raining fish and you're left thinking, "What in the world is going on?"
The way Murakami weaves in all this weird, surreal stuff with the everyday stuff - it's absolute genius. You've got Kafka, this 15-year-old kid, running away from home, and then you've got Nakata, this old dude who can talk to cats. And somehow, SOMEHOW, Murakami makes it all work together like it's the most natural thing in the world.
And the music, man. The way Murakami writes about music - it's like he's plugging the melodies straight into your brain. He'll be describing some classical piece, and you can almost hear it, even if you've never listened to classical music in your life. It's not just background noise either - the music's woven into the story, into the characters' lives. It's like... it's like the soundtrack to their souls or some deep stuff like that.
But here's the thing that really got me - underneath all the crazy, otherworldly stuff, Murakami's hitting you with these deep truths about life. Like, you can't run away from yourself, no matter how far you go. Kafka thinks he's escaping his destiny by leaving home, but he's really running straight towards it. And Nakata, man - that guy's journey is all about accepting who he is, weird cat-talking abilities and all.
The way Murakami deals with memory and identity - it's mind-blowing. He's got these characters grappling with who they are, with their past, with their desires. And it's messy as hell, just like real life. There's no neat resolution, no "and they all lived happily ever after" nonsense. It's complex, it's confusing, it leaves you with more questions than answers - but isn't that just like life?
By the time I finished this book, I felt like I'd been on some kind of hallucinogenic trip. My brain was scrambled, but in the best possible way. It's like Murakami reached into my head, rearranged all the furniture, and left me to figure out where everything goes. And you know what? I absolutely loved it.
This book - it's not just a story. It's an experience. It's a journey into the weird, wonderful, messed-up landscape of human existence. And Murakami? He's not just a writer - he's a magician, weaving reality and fantasy together until you can't tell where one ends and the other begins.
I'm telling you, Kafka on the Shore is the kind of book that stays with you. It's been days since I finished it, and I'm still finding myself thinking about it at random moments. It's like... it's like Murakami's opened up this door in my brain, and now I can't close it. And you know what? I don't want to. Because the world on the other side of that door? It's weird as heck, but it's beautiful too. And it feels more real than reality sometimes.

Title: Conversations with Friends
Author: Sally Rooney
My Review:
It's not like you can just break down Rooney's work into easy bits, you know? Before this, I'd only read Normal People, and fuck me if I wasn't completely thrown by her style. The way she gets into people's heads with such simple words - it's not as easy as she makes it look. It's messy, it's fucked up sometimes, but that's kinda the point......
Conversations with Friends is cut from the same cloth, but this time we're dealing with four people's shit instead of two. The writing's a bit different from Normal People, but then again, this was her first rodeo. What really got me was how real the dialogue felt, like I was eavesdropping on actual people's lives......
Rooney's got this knack for getting that human relationships and the mind are these fragile, complex things. You can't just explain them away with some neat little bow. People in love? They're fucking irrational. And attraction? That's a wild card you can't control for shit.
Throughout the book, I kept feeling off-kilter. Rooney treats relationships like they're these casual, almost disposable things people do without thinking, but then BAM - she hits you with this raw vulnerability that just floors you. It's genius, really.
The ending's all blurry lines and question marks. Take Frances - she's this walking bundle of insecurities, but she's still going back for more with Nick, even though it's probably gonna fuck her up emotionally. It's like watching a car crash in slow motion, but you get why she's doing it.
In the end, it's just this everyday story about people and their messy-as-hell relationships. And maybe that's why it worked for me - 'cause that's how life actually is, you know? It's not all grand gestures and fairy tale endings. It's complicated, it's painful, it's beautiful in its own fucked-up way. And Rooney? She gets that. She really fucking gets it......and to be fair I got disturbed a little but its okay....Books are supposed to do that....

Title: Birthday Girl

My Review:
"Birthday Girl" is a masterclass in subtle storytelling that lingers long after you've turned the final page. As I finished reading, I found myself pondering, "What did the girl actually wish for on her 20th birthday?" It wasn't until several minutes later that the brilliance of Murakami's craft truly dawned on me.

In this deceptively simple tale, Murakami weaves a narrative that defies straightforward interpretation. He doesn't spoon-feed answers to his readers; instead, he invites us to dive into the depths of our own imagination and extract personal meaning from the story's enigmatic core.
The beauty of "Birthday Girl" lies in its ability to spark contemplation. It's a story that reveals itself gradually, layer by layer, with each subsequent reading. Murakami's restrained prose belies the complexity of the themes he explores – the weight of choices, the passage from youth to adulthood, and the tantalizing allure of "what ifs" that shape our lives.

What struck me most was how Murakami managed to create such a thought-provoking piece with so few words. The story's brevity is deceptive; it's a literary seed that, once planted in the reader's mind, grows into a forest of possibilities and interpretations. It's a must read !!!!!

Title: Men Without Women
Author: Haruki Murakami
Additional Authors: Phillip Gabriel, Ted Goossen, Chip Kidd
My Review:
Haruki Murakami's short story collection, "Men Without Women," is a profound exploration of the male psyche, drenched in themes of love, loss, and loneliness. In each story, Murakami delves into the complexities of relationships, particularly the enigmatic nature of understanding women, and the inherent loneliness that men experience.

Drive My Car: This story sets the tone for the collection, blending the idea that men in love are simple by nature. Murakami suggests that understanding a woman is far more challenging than rocket science and that every man harbors a blind spot in his relationships. Through Kafuku's story, whose wife cheated on him despite their love, Murakami illustrates the bewildering behavior of people close to us and emphasizes that understanding another person's heart is a lifelong journey that begins with understanding our own.

Yesterday: In "Yesterday," Murakami poignantly portrays how life passes us by, often leaving us to realize what we've lost only in retrospect. This story echoes the sentiment that we often fail to appreciate the "good old days" until they are behind us, mirroring a poignant dialogue from "The Office." The narrative captures the inevitability of change and the nostalgic longing for the past.

Scheherazade: In this mesmerizing tale, Murakami introduces us to Habara, a man who lives in self-imposed isolation. His only contact with the outside world is through a woman he calls Scheherazade, after the legendary storyteller from "One Thousand and One Nights." Scheherazade visits him regularly, providing not just necessities but also enchanting stories of her past. Through this relationship, Murakami explores themes of dependence, the power of storytelling, and the deep human need for connection. The story within a story format highlights the layers of narrative and reality, ultimately revealing that even in isolation, human connections are vital and profoundly impactful.

Kino: Through Kino's story, Murakami explores the delayed recognition of personal pain. Kino, a simple man, only comes to terms with his hurt long after his wife leaves him. This delayed emotional response highlights the deep-seated loneliness that can persist despite outward appearances.

Samsa in Love: This story serves as an ode to Kafka, expanding on the absurdity of human existence. Murakami juxtaposes the surreal transformation of Gregor Samsa into an insect with the everyday absurdities humans face, suggesting that despite our lack of understanding, we strive to maintain control over our lives.

Men Without Women: The collection culminates with metaphors and symbols, such as unicorns, to depict how men become men without women. Murakami illustrates the paradox of men living lonely lives despite being in relationships, haunted by the loss of the "one" woman who truly mattered. These men, though they harbor no regrets, wish peace for the women they have lost, even after death.Throughout "Men Without Women," Murakami masterfully portrays the vulnerability of men. His characters navigate the nuanced emotions of love, loss, and grief, revealing the jewels of understanding they gain through their solitary journeys.

Murakami's genius lies in his ability to craft characters that resonate deeply, offering readers a mirror to their own experiences of loneliness and longing.In this collection, Murakami vividly demonstrates that life is not circular. Instead, it is a linear progression where the emotional puzzle is never truly complete without the essential piece that is a woman. His portrayal of male vulnerability and the emotional landscapes of his characters solidifies his status as a literary genius, making "Men Without Women" a must-read for those seeking to understand the intricacies of the human heart.

My Review: "Norwegian Wood" was my introduction to Murakami, and it captivated me with its vivid imagery and emotional depth. As I read, I felt like I was watching a film unfold before my eyes. The writing is fresh and filled with emotions we often overlook. Murakami's depiction of depression and the longing for love is masterful. I read somewhere that Murakami himself questions why this work became famous, yet it resonates deeply with human experience.The journey of Toru and his feelings is profoundly real. He doesn’t fully understand love, but he is constantly consumed by thoughts of it. He tries to comprehend, but is always taken aback by the unpredictability of life. To long for something and cope with its absence is an art that Murakami captures beautifully. The ambiguous ending leaves readers perplexed about what happened to Toru after the phone call at the station with Midori.Murakami, in my view, illustrates the idea that "Beauty is terror." It might seem intriguing, but as you observe closely, you see that everything beautiful and admirable can make you quiver. This book made me realize how love can be tangible, reaching the heights of the highest peak. We remember our first love because it shows us the undeniable truth that we can love and be loved in return, even if imperfectly. Love, in all its messy, beautiful glory, shapes who we are and helps us understand ourselves more deeply.

Title: Normal People
Author: Sally Rooney
My Review:
Does the sadness that appears in us while we saunter through life have a meaning, or is it just a ramification of our deep thoughts towards our own desires and dreams we put forth?

Sally Rooney, in this book, dives deep into two such characters who by any measure can't be considered normal people. Yet the title is "Normal People," maybe because we see growth amid confusion. Connell, though having a huge problem in communication, is somehow understood by Marianne. This book is almost opposite of all love stories that exist, yet its peculiarity has a profound idea of wholesomeness in it which cannot be avoided. It's a little frustrating to read the characters being depressed and sad all the time, but it is comforting to know that it resonates with reality. We all are sad, but we hide those parts well enough and live in denial. The power that Connell and Marianne had on each other may feel somewhat weird but is understandable for the fact that sometimes people find someone so comforting, like home, that they keep coming back though they wander off for a brief period of time. The book hits pangs of confusion that resonated with me because of the confusions that I keep having in my life. Sally Rooney's non-linear writing makes the story most interesting because we feel like we're watching two people lay out their vulnerability, yet somehow go on living life despite pain. That is hope, and to me, this book is all about telling the world that even the most unusual people can have love. Though it may seem odd to others, it exists. The ending is ambiguous, but when Marianne says she will always be there, it gives you the idea of how she has grown from having shallowness inside her to having some idea of fulfillment. It's one of the best reads for me, though I know it made me think some sad thoughts, yet prolific ideas that love in its most unusual form is like early monsoon... Glowy but in a low-key way, is a blessing to scornful summer in life.

Title: The Metamorphosis
Author: Franz Kafka
My Review:
The story awakens us to the metamorphic hell of Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman who one morning finds himself inexplicably transformed into a monstrous verminous creature. With strokes of genius, Kafka inverts our comfortable reality, thrusting us into an absurdist purgatory. We inhabit Gregor’s alienated consciousness, his insectoid form rendering him an object of revulsion to his own family. Their alienating cruelty slices like razored accusations against the soul.

For is this not the deepest ache of the self — to be utterly isolated, divorced from the kinship and societal belonging we innately crave ?

Kafka wields his protagonist’s bizarre curse as an indictment of the shallow attachments we forge. When otherness disrupts our mundane roles and facades, the depths of our self-absorption are laid bare. We are all too willing to sacrifice those closest at the altar of shallow conformity, severing bonds once held sacred when abnormality rears its unsettling head.

The transformation of Gregor Samsa is not merely physical but deeply psychological. It is a manifestation of the profound alienation he feels in a world that values him solely for his utility. Once a dutiful son and hardworking salesman, Gregor’s metamorphosis strips him of his role and renders him an outcast, a grotesque embodiment of the fears and anxieties that plague modern existence. The reaction of his family — ranging from horror to outright rejection — mirrors society’s ruthless dismissal of those who no longer fit into its rigid, materialistic framework.

Kafka’s narrative is a stark critique of the materialistic world, where the worth of an individual is measured by their productivity and conformity. When Gregor can no longer fulfill his role, he is discarded, a disturbing commentary on how society abandons those who are no longer deemed useful. This brutal reality resonates with a profound sense of betrayal and despair, as the wounds inflicted by those closest to us cut the deepest. The family, supposed to be a sanctuary of unconditional love, becomes a microcosm of a society that prizes conformity over compassion, material success over human connection.

With hypnotic poetic lucidity, Kafka dissects the materialistic myopia poisoning the human spirit in its perpetual grasping for the baubles of status, wealth, and empty illusions of purpose. All that we cloak our aimless lives in unravels with Gregor’s transfiguration into abhorrent insect form. Family, societal esteem, personal identity — these traditions and values turn to ash under Kafka’s scathing lens.

The unholy truth blooms — absent the superficial roles we assign ourselves, we are all grotesque impostors scurrying across existence’s barren rock.

Kafka’s use of imagery and allegory elevates his storytelling to a realm where the personal becomes universal. Gregor’s insect form, repulsive yet pitiable, symbolizes the dehumanization and isolation that arise from societal expectations. His confinement to his room mirrors the internal prisons we build within ourselves, walls that grow higher with each unspoken fear and unrealized dream. The decaying apple lodged in Gregor’s back, a wound inflicted by his father, represents the enduring pain of familial rejection and the slow, inevitable decline into oblivion.

It is a sobering vision, yet one imbued with cold profundity. By peeling away our delusional realities layer by nightmarish layer, Kafka affirms the nihilistic essence at the core of our being. We are hapless creatures scuttling from one invented mirage to the next — from lovers to careers to families to personal philosophies, each a gossamer veil obscuring the underlying emptiness. All unravels, all crumbles to dust when our agreed-upon fantasies implode and the Meaninglessness howls in bare-boned rebuke.

Reading Kafka is an experience that forces introspection, compelling us to question the very nature of our existence. His stories are not merely tales of individual suffering but profound meditations on the human condition. They evoke a sense of Kafkaesque dread, a term that has come to denote situations that are nightmarishly complex, bizarre, and illogical. This style bears a resemblance to the Russian story “The Nose” by Nikolai Gogol, where a man’s nose leaves his face and leads an independent life, embodying the absurdity and fragmentation of human identity. Life, in Kafka’s universe, is absurd and often cruel. It is a world where logic is subverted, and the only certainty is uncertainty itself. Yet, in this bleak landscape, there is a strange, haunting beauty.

Kafka’s prose, with its meticulous detail and stark clarity, captures the ephemeral nature of existence and the quiet desperation that lies at the heart of human experience. This is the existential abyss Kafka ever steers us towards in his multi-layered, hallucinatory parables. His works epitomize what has become known as “Kafkaesque” — a realm where the nonsensical reigns, where unfeeling bureaucracies entrap the self, and nightmarish reality blurs all boundaries between absurdity and quotidian despair. It is a harrowing, intoxicating realm where the enormity of our profound aloneness is cast in searing illumination — as exhilarating as it is shattering to confront.

To drink deep from Kafka’s opus is to be forever disquieted, our perception of the world around us rendered fundamentally unshackled. We move henceforth with a perpetual glimmer of disbelieving awe at the surreal delirium underlying the thin fictions we cling to. We sense the pulsating potential for all to metamorphose into macabre travesty in a blink of cosmic caprice. Franz Kafka’s literary sorcery envelops the reader in a murmuring disquietude — his parables reflecting and rebounding infinitely, their dark truth eclipsing with each frantic heartbeat. Reality was never more tenuous, the abyss never more intoxicating.
